top_choice_rationale: P001 (B005: Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn) does best on the common test. The random-coefficients demand framework with endogenous prices changed what can be credibly known about substitution, market power and merger effects. It has about three decades of use and critique in merger review, antitrust, regulation, trade, health and environmental work. The credit core is one jointly authored contribution that maps onto three names, and no prior-prize overlap has been raised. The citation should be kept to demand and competition estimation and be honest that it rewards a method, not settled empirical magnitudes. Sensitivity to functional form and instruments qualifies how the estimates are used but not the originality of the method. The exclusion of Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin is a real cost of the three-name cap. I rank P002 (B030: Autor, Hanson, Dorn) second. It has strong design-based evidence and a clean trio, but the persistence, magnitude and shift-share debates make it less mature, and it is adjacent to recent prizes. I still place it above P000, because it is a substantive, well-attributed achievement and does not fail the bar. This is my own weighing, not a count of supporters. I have not independently verified the replication records or prior-prize claims in the files.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. My profile lists no collaboration or institutional tie to Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn, Autor, Hanson or Dorn. My co-authors (Kaplan, Axelson, Weisbach, Jenkinson, Lerner, Sørensen, Robinson and others) are not among the credited names. My field is corporate finance and contracting, which is not adjacent to B005 or B030. I disclose my Chicago Booth adjunct post and my long committee overlap with Hassler, Krusell, Ellingsen and Svensson, and I do not adjudicate them.
